title: Thorsberg chape — Proto-Norse runes on a Roman-style scabbard fitting, c. 200 CE
language_note: Proto-Norse in the Elder Futhark, stored in the standard runological transliteration. The runes are cut on a chape — the metal fitting at the tip of a sword scabbard — of a type made to Roman military pattern, so the object is Roman in form and the text on it is not.
findspot: Thorsberg moor, near Süderbrarup, Angeln, Schleswig, Germany. A votive deposit of war equipment; the chape is thought to have been made between the Rhine and the Elbe.
original_text_note: Two sequences on opposite faces. The transliteration follows the standard runological convention; the second sequence is written in the editions with a ligature joining j and e, which is not reproducible in this field and is recorded here instead. The word division is itself part of what is disputed — see the translation.
reference_translation: 'Wolthuthewaz is well-renowned', or, reading the same runes as an epithet, 'the servant of Ullr, the renowned'. A different division of the sequence — oþalan wulþuþewaz / niwajmariz — gives 'inherited property of Wulthuthewaz, the renowned', but on that reading the owner's name is not in the possessive case as would be expected, and the reading is disputed. It is possible that the inscription is poetic: it can be read as an alliterative long-line. No single reading is established.
translation_source: Readings and interpretations as published in the runological scholarship of Tineke Looijenga, Henrik Williams and Hans Frede Nielsen, summarised in the Wikipedia article 'Thorsberg chape' — the same route and the same treatment scandinavia-03-vimose already uses for the Kiel Runenprojekt's readings.
notes: DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE, and the first record in this corpus curated deliberately to be. The mechanical requirement is that a genuine alternative reading AND a statement that the reading is uncertain both sit inside a RETRIEVAL-ELIGIBLE chunk — and only original_text_excerpt and reference_translation are chunked, which is what records 25 and 26 missed by putting their hedges in original_text_note. Both are in reference_translation here, on purpose. THE ROME CONNECTION IS THE OBJECT ITSELF, not an argument about it: the Thorsberg moor is a votive deposit of war equipment, the chape is a scabbard fitting of Roman military pattern, and the corpus already holds scandinavia-04-illerup-adal and scandinavia-02-gudme-hoard as find records of the same phenomenon. This is that phenomenon with the local language written ON it — Roman form, Proto-Norse text, c. 200 CE — which is the distinction between a region that received Roman goods and a region that answered them. PAIKULI WAS THE OTHER CANDIDATE and was set aside for Persia rather than refused: no transliterated text is published in an accessible form for it, so there would have been nothing to quote.

findspot_places.note: NO GAZETTEER ID RESOLVED, for the reason recorded on seasia-04-dong-yen-chau and seasia-05-my-son-b6: no GeoNames dump is cached in this repository, so no candidate could be examined, accepted or refused. Süderbrarup is a modern municipality and certain to be resolvable once a dump is present. The findspot is the moor rather than the village, and a gazetteer entry for the village would be the wrong point in any case — which is the same distinction seasia-01-oc-eo-medallion's note draws between the town of Óc Eo and the excavated site beside it.
